newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: CAPE YORK COMPENSATION COULD BE HUGE SAYS ABORIGINAL LEADER
Cape York Land Council chairman, Noel Pearson, says native title compensation for the Cape York Peninsula could cost taxpayers up to $2 billion.

Mr Pearson says the Federal Government needs to consider the financial implications of the compensation issue more carefully. He says the amount of any compensation under native title will be based on the freehold value of the land plus administration costs.
VICTORIA CALLS FOR FRUIT BAN TO BE LIFTED
The Victorian Government has called on New South Wales and Queensland to lift bans on the import of Victorian apples and pears.
Tests on all orchards and nurseries in country Victoria have found no trace of fireblight disease.
Even though tests haven't been completed on suspected fireblight samples from Melbourne's Botanic Gardens, Victoria's Agriculture Minister, Pat MacNamara, hopes interstate bans will now be lifted.
He's declared Victoria's fruit-growing regions fireblight-free, and says the fruit should get full market access.
The bans have already cost hundreds of jobs in the Goulburn Valley, Australia's main pear-producing region.
TOURISM DOWNTURN AT MAJOR CENTRES
Cairns and the Gold Coast have been identified as the tourist centres hurting most from a decline in tourism growth in Australia.
The key markets of Japan, Taiwan, the US and Germany are softening, prompting the tourist commission to announce new initiatives to promote Australia internationally.
At an international travel trade fair in Melbourne, Commission head John Morse said traditional Australian destinations must respond to changing travelling habits.
He says the downturn may be a result of too great a reliance on too few markets, and he is urging all sectors of the tourism industry to rethink their strategies.
POLICE PROBE LEAKS OF OVERSEAS CABLES TO MEDIA
Australian Foreign Affairs Officials say the results of a police investigation into alleged leaks of confidential overseas cables to the media this year, will be made public.
Senior diplomats have told a Senate Committee hearing today the leak of four cables to the media has been referred to the Australian Federal Police.

Labor Senator Peter Cook told the committee that between February and March this year articles were published in the Australia press allegedly based on confidential cables from Australian emabassies in China, Moscow, Indonesia and New Zealand.
The first discussed the New Zealand governments' stance on East Timor.
The second reported sensitive comments by the Foriegn Affairs Secretary, Phillip Flood, on China's approach to the human rights dialogue with Australia.
The third referred to discussions with Indonesia's Foreign Minister, Ali Atlas on Australia's participation in the Asia-Europe summit.
A fourth article claimed it was based on a cable leaked from the Moscow embassy and was concerned President Yeltsin's health.
